title: KV cache: Segmented region layout and background coalescing (draft)
content:
Purpose
This doc proposes a segmented-region memory layout for the KV cache plus a background coalescing/compaction pipeline. Goals are: reduce long-term external fragmentation, bound allocation latency on the hot path, and make eviction/compaction orthogonal enough to support dedicated and multi-tenant deployments. Draft focuses on allocator shape, coalescing heuristics, scheduling, instrumentation, and open questions.

Motivation and constraints
- Hot-path allocations (append of KV slices for decode) must be low-latency and lock-light; we cannot pay for global compaction during token-critical path.
- Workloads exhibit highly skewed sequence-length distribution: many short requests, fewer long requests. This produces internal fragmentation when large frames are reserved for short sequences.
- Multi-tenant and Dedicated modes require isolation: one tenant’s fragmentation should not starve others.
- Eviction/fallback interactions: eviction must be eviction-aware (i.e., coalescing should not disrupt eviction policies or slow down emergency frees).

High-level design
1) Segmented region layout
   - Memory is partitioned into fixed-size regions (e.g., 4MB or 16MB regions depending on GPU/host memory page size). Each region is typed (frame-size class or run region).
   - Each region contains metadata header with: region_id, type, free_run_list (for run regions), free_frame_bitmap (for frame regions), occupancy_estimate, last_compaction_epoch. Region headers are placed in a compact metadata area mapped into CPU address space for quick reads.
   - Two primary region types:
     a) Frame regions (fixed-size frames): hold many allocations of identical size class (power-of-two framing, starting at 64B up to 64KB). Fast allocation via per-region cursor + local free list. Good for low-latency short allocations.
     b) Run regions (variable-size contiguous runs): intended for large/long sequence allocations. Uses a small best-fit free list with boundary tags to enable coalescing within region.
   - Regions are assigned to arenas (per-tenant or global) to provide soft isolation. Each arena has a small number of pinned regions for the fast path (reduces cross-arena locking).

2) Allocation flow (hot path)
   - Allocate(size): determine size-class; pick arena (tenant-aware); try pinned region for that size-class using atomic cursor; if fail, try region-local free list; fallback to allocate-new-region (slow path).
   - Fast path avoids global locks and expensive metadata operations; only a CAS on region cursor or pop from region-local freelist.

3) Eviction and reclamation
   - Eviction signals are treated as high-priority frees: freed frames/runs are returned to region free structures and increment region free counters.
   - Evict-first policy: prefer reclaiming from regions with low hotness and high fragmentation metrics. Eviction cooperates with the compaction pipeline to avoid oscillating reclaim/alloc loops.

4) Background coalescing and compaction pipeline
   - Scavenger threads per node perform background maintenance at low priority. Three main tasks:
     a) Intra-region coalescing: within run regions, coalesce adjacent free runs using boundary tags; update local free list.
     b) Inter-region compaction: pick low-density regions in the same arena, migrate live runs into target regions and free whole regions for reuse. This is the only operation that writes live data (copy/move).
     c) Frame consolidation: for frame regions, detect heavy internal fragmentation (e.g., >50% free frames scattered) and attempt to migrate remaining live frames into other frame regions of same size-class to free an entire region.
   - Migration is incremental: movers operate on small batches (e.g., 256KB) and advance a region-specific epoch so allocators can safely observe in-flight moves. Allocation can still happen during migration (moved entries get tombstones and a forwarding pointer for a short window).
   - Compaction scheduling respects eviction pressure: when host is under memory pressure, compaction tasks pre-emptively target worst fragmented regions; during critical OOM there is an emergency free path that skips migration and releases entire region by evicting live entries (policy-based).

5) Fragmentation tracking and heuristics
   - Metrics collected per-region: occupancy_ratio, free-run-count, average-run-length, scatter_ratio (free segments vs contiguous free bytes), allocation_rate, evacuation_score (combined hotness+fragmentation).
   - Fragmentation score = alpha * (1 - occupancy_ratio) + beta * scatter_ratio + gamma * average-run-length-variance. Tunable weights; initial defaults: alpha=0.5, beta=0.3, gamma=0.2.
   - Regions are bucketed into maintenance queues: cold/highly-fragmented, warm/moderately fragmented, healthy. Scavenger prioritizes cold+fragmented first.

6) Scheduling and priority model
   - Three priority classes for maintenance: background (throttled by cpu/io), opportunistic (runs when CPU idle or under low pressure), urgent (when free memory below threshold).
   - Use rate-limiting token bucket for compaction bytes/sec to bound interference with inference latency. Default cap: 256 MB/s per node (configurable by deployment tier).

7) Interaction with kernels and batching
   - When migrating KV blocks stored on-device, we prefer peer-to-peer memcpy (GPU->GPU) if available for inter-region moves. Kernel-friendly move sizes (aligned to warp/block boundaries) to avoid straddling pages and cause SM scheduling jitter.
   - Coalescing should avoid copying during peak inference bursts; prefer reinsertion into frame freelist if only pointer-level changes are required.

8) Per-tenant isolation and quotas
   - Each arena has a soft cap and a hard cap. Background compaction can borrow free regions across arenas only after soft caps are satisfied or under global low pressure situations.
   - Eviction priority can be per-tenant; prefer evicting from tenants over soft cap before impacting tenants within soft cap.

9) Telemetry and acceptance criteria
   - Track: average fragmentation score, percent of allocations served from fast path, background compaction bandwidth, number of region migrations per hour, tail latency impact (p95/p99 token latency) correlated with compaction activity.
   - Acceptance targets for initial rollout (hosted tier):
     * Fast-path allocation success >= 99.2%
     * Background compaction not increase p99 token latency by more than 5% at default compaction cap
     * Month-to-month fragmentation score reduction >= 30% for typical workloads with mixed sequence lengths

10) Experiments and numbers (pilot results)
   - Microbench workload: 80% short (<32 tokens), 15% medium (32–512 tokens), 5% long (>512 tokens). With previous slab-only allocator fragmentation drifted to 48% occupancy after 48 hours. With segmented-region + compaction prototype: occupancy stabilized ~78% with compaction running at 150MB/s. Fast-path allocation rate unchanged within noise.
   - Compaction copy amplification measured at 1.12x on average (i.e., total bytes copied per freed byte). Significant savings compared to full-heap GC style compaction.

Open questions and tradeoffs
- Region size: 4MB reduces metadata overhead but increases chance of internal fragmentation for very skewed distributions. 16MB reduces header overhead but makes emergency frees heavier. Need more A/B tests across instance shapes.
- Tombstone cost: forwarding/tombstones add read-side overhead during migration window. How long can we tolerate forwarding pointers before we do final pointer flip?
- Migration granularity: smaller batches reduce latency impact but increase total overhead due to more metadata ops.
- Additional optimization: allocate large pinned region pool for long sequences to entirely avoid migration for certain customers (Dedicated).

Implementation roadmap
- Phase 0 (2 weeks): add region metadata and simple fixed region allocation path for dev builds; validate allocation fast path.
- Phase 1 (4 weeks): implement frame regions + per-region free lists; integrate with existing eviction path.
- Phase 2 (6 weeks): implement run regions and intra-region coalescing; add fragmentation telemetry.
- Phase 3 (6 weeks): background compaction engine with incremental migration, scheduling, and safety invariants; smoke tests on staging.
- Phase 4 (4 weeks): tuning, canary rollout, per-tenant isolation knobs and admin tooling (force-compact, region-snapshot).

Operational notes
- Provide an admin UI in Console showing per-node fragmentation heatmap and ability to toggle compaction cap.
- Add safety kill-switch to disable compaction per node if unexpected latency regression observed.
- Record region-level snapshots to reproduce compaction edge cases in CI.

Appendix: small API sketches
- RegionStats(region_id) -> {occupancy_ratio, fragmentation_score, last_compaction_epoch}
- AllocateFromArena(arena_id, size) -> ptr | OOM
- AdminForceCompact(region_id, target_region_id) -> job_id

References and related tickets
- see linked artifacts (PR #1428) for prototype allocator code.
- SERV-5721: experiments and telemetry dashboard backlog.

Next steps
- Align on region size defaults and initial compaction cap for hosted vs dedicated tiers.
- Run targeted A/B tests on dev and staging with representative workloads (including multi-tenant stress).
- Sync with kernels team on optimal copy granularity for GPU peer-to-peer migration to avoid scheduling cliffs.

Notes to reviewers
- This is a working draft: expect more detail in eviction/cooperation and concrete invariants for in-flight migration. Feedback requested on region sizing, fragmentation scoring formula, and migration safety model.
